title: The river from the Temple (Ezekiel 47:1–12)
hook: a river deepens and heals the salt sea; everything lives where it goes

segments.voice: Yesterday, two sticks, Judah and Joseph, joined into one in the prophet's hand. Today, the last of our days in Ezekiel.

Ankles. Knees. Waist. Then water to swim in. Near the end of his book, Ezekiel is shown a vision of the Temple rebuilt, and his guide brings him back to the door of the house. There's water seeping out from under the threshold, flowing east. A trickle. The guide walks out with a measuring line, measures a distance, and leads Ezekiel through: the water is to his ankles. Another measure: to his knees. Another: to his loins. Another, and it's a river he can't cross, waters to swim in.
screen: `WATER UNDER THE THRESHOLD.` → `ANKLES, KNEES, WAIST.` → `A RIVER TOO DEEP TO CROSS.`

segments.voice: Water that seeps out under a door usually spreads out and soaks away. This water does the opposite. With no stream feeding it that the text mentions, it keeps getting deeper. Then the guide asks Ezekiel a question: son of man, hast thou seen this? He's brought back along the bank, and now he sees very many trees on both sides. The river flows down into the desert and into the sea, and the waters are healed. Here's the line the whole chapter turns on, in the King James words: "every thing shall live whither the river cometh." Fishermen will stand on the shore and spread their nets, and the fish will be many. The trees along the banks will bear fruit every month, and their leaves won't wither. And the last detail: "the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine." Food and healing, from water that started under a door. Ezekiel's book began with exiles sitting by a foreign river, the Chebar, far from the Temple. Near its end, a river flows out from the Temple, so deep it can't be crossed, bringing life even to the sea. Some readers hear it as God's presence flowing out from the house. And notice where it starts: not as a river at all, but as a seep under a door, measured again and again as it goes.
screen: `A SEEP UNDER THE DOOR.` · `IT KEEPS GETTING DEEPER.` · then, large: `EVERY THING SHALL LIVE WHITHER THE RIVER COMETH.` · then: `FRUIT FOR MEAT, LEAF FOR MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Find something in your life that's still at the ankles: a practice you just started, a new friendship, something you're learning, maybe even this daily habit. Without pushing, picture walking a little farther in, ankles, then knees, and let the breath be the measuring line, one length at a time. If you pray, you can ask that it bring life where it goes.
Chebar, the foreign river where Ezekiel's exiles once sat, far from the Temple whose own river later heals the sea. Today's word.
Your line: everything lives where it flows. Even a trickle can become a river. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 47 within the book's closing vision of a rebuilt Temple (chapters 40–48), and the Talmud remembers Hananiah ben Hezekiah working through those chapters to reconcile their laws with the Torah's.

chat.says: Ezekiel's book starts by one river and ends by another. Why does that matter?
options: Exiles sat by the Chebar far from the Temple; later a river flows from it, healing the sea.
Both rivers are the Chebar, so the exiles never really left Babylon at all.
The Temple river dries up, showing the exiles would never be healed.
chat.meaning: The book opens by a foreign river, far from the Temple, and near its end a river from the Temple brings life wherever it comes.

Chebar.meaning: a river in Babylon where the exiles sat

Ezekiel.meaning: a priest and prophet among the exiles in Babylon

son of man.meaning: how Ezekiel is addressed: simply, a human being

notes: The text gives the measurements as a thousand cubits each (47:3–5); the script leaves the number out.
'With no stream feeding it that the text mentions' is an observation on the text; Keeper may want to check.
Torah compared to water: a common rabbinic image (e.g. Taanit 7a); kept general.
Final Ezekiel day; tomorrow begins the Twelve.
